title: Sluggish thermochemical basal mantle structures support their long-lived stability

paper_content.abstract: Large low shear-wave velocity provinces (LLSVPs) in the lowermost mantle are the largest geological structures on Earth, but their origin and age remain highly enigmatic. Geological constraints suggest the stability of the LLSVPs since at least 200 million years ago. Here, we conduct numerical modeling of mantle convection with plate-like behavior that yields a Pacific-like girdle of mantle downwelling which successfully forms two antipodal basal mantle structures similar to the LLSVPs. Our parameterized results optimized to reflect LLSVP features exhibit velocities for the basal mantle structures that are ~4 times slower than the ambient mantle if they are thermochemical, while the velocity is similar to the ambient mantle if purely thermal. The sluggish motion of the thermochemical basal mantle structures in our models permits the notion that geological data from hundreds of millions of years ago are related to modern LLSVPs as they are essentially stationary over such time scales.
paper_content.introduction:
The makeup and origins of Earth’s deep and inaccessible interior have long been mysterious. Ever since the detection by seismic tomography of the two antipodal large low shear-wave velocity provinces (LLSVPs) — regions in the lowermost mantle in which the shear-wave velocity is lower than that of the ambient mantle1 — their origin has been extensively debated. Although a purely thermal origin of LLSVPs cannot be excluded2, multiple sources of geophysical data indicate that the LLSVPs are thermally hot and should also be chemically distinct3–6. Whether the LLSVPs derive most or part of their density from a primordial layer of dense materials (such as from the crystallization of magma ocean7 or moon-forming giant impact8) and/or a layer of subducted oceanic crust growing over time, the antiquity of their current morphology into two piles most likely developed at some later point in Earth’s history1. Yet despite great advances in recent decades, many features of the LLSVPs remain enigmatic. There is a great debate about the stability and antiquity of the LLSVPs. In general, there are two end-member interpretations where the LLSVPs are fixed, ancient structures9,10 or dynamic, young structures11–13.

Various types of geological data appear to suggest the African LLSVP has been essentially fixed since 200–300 million years ago (Ma) (i.e., supercontinent Pangaea age), including large igneous provinces (LIPs)10, palaeogeography14, and net characteristics of plate motions15. Some studies have even argued for LLSVP stability back to >500 Ma or even since early in Earth’s history9,16. Alternatively, recent work has challenged LLSVP stability as far back as ca. 200–300 Ma Pangaea age. Numerical modeling of basal mantle structures (BMSs; referring to LLSVPs created in models) parameterized by plate kinematics and thus the mobility of subduction zones at the surface and slabs sinking into the mantle suggest that the lower mantle is more dynamic than previously considered12. Although BMSs are suggested to be very actively dynamic in recent studies, this conclusion is based on imposed plate reconstructions whose accuracy decreases back in time12. Therefore, a fully dynamic approach provides a viable alternative approach.

In this study, we conduct numerical modeling of BMSs to assess their mobility under self-consistent mantle convection with plate-like lithospheric behavior as the top boundary condition. We explore the parameter space that does or does not permit the creation of two antipodal BMSs akin to the areal extent of the LLSVPs. Those results that successfully satisfy such criteria are able to constrain the relative velocity of the BMSs and the ambient mantle, thereby testing the validity of LLSVP stability on 100 million years (Myr) and 1 billion years (Gyr) timescales as both have been proposed by competing models.
paper_content.results:
Role of plate tectonics in the topology of basal mantle structures
Three-dimensional thermochemical mantle convection models in spherical geometry on the Yin-Yang grid17,18 were conducted with plastic yielding to generate plate boundaries at the top19,20 and an initially even basal layer of dense materials in an attempt to generate BMSs over an evolutionary period of 4.56 Gyrs (comparable to the history of the Earth; “Methods”). As our goal is to investigate the stability time scale of LLSVPs, we first investigate the reaction of the topology of BMSs to plate tectonics by varying the strength of the oceanic lithosphere. We then analyze the mobility of BMSs in an Earth-like model where a Pacific-like subduction girdle and antipodal degree-2 BMSs form.

In our models, slabs penetrate into the lower mantle21 and push aside the BMSs. When plastic yielding is taken into account, two antipodal BMSs are split by a great subduction girdle (Fig. 1d), which is consistent with the present-day Earth where the two LLSVPs are separated by the Pacific “ring of fire” of subduction at the surface as well as with previous 3D models12,22. In 2D convection models with plastic yielding, two antipodal slabs could cut the layered BMSs and then push them into two piles22. In our work, we achieve a 3-D Earth-like model with quasi-stationary BMSs that maintain degree-2 structure for about 630 Myrs when yield stress is set to 100 MPa (Fig. 1d).

To evaluate the influence of plate tectonics on BMSs, we vary the yield stress, hence the strength of the oceanic lithosphere from 10–200 MPa, which controls the plate tectonics configuration20. Figure 1 shows snapshots of the surface viscosity, BMSs, plumes, and subduction. In our series of models, the observed planforms can be divided into four groups. (i) Ultra-low yield stress (30 MPa) yields four subduction systems that stir BMSs, and no piles are observed on the CMB. (ii) Low yield stress (50 MPa) yields a triple-junction-like subduction zone that is concentrated in a semi-sphere and cannot migrate because of the hindering of intense upwelling from the margin or interior of the one-pile BMS with high topography. (iii) Intermediate yield stress (70–100 MPa) yields more than one subduction girdle that cuts the BMSs and pushes them into two piles, where the distance between them increases with increasing yield stress. (iv) High yield stress (200 MPa) yields one circular pile that is pushed against by the downwelling. We further find that successful Earth-like models with two antipodal piles covering the CMB with areas of ~25% similar to LLSVPs occur in our study within a narrow range of moderate yield stress (90–100 MPa) (Fig. 2).

More sluggish thermochemical LLSVPs than thermal LLSVPs
To quantify the mobility of LLSVPs, we calculate the horizontal velocities of BMSs and the ambient mantle in our simulations (Fig. 3). The horizontal velocities of the BMSs are ~4 times slower than that of the ambient mantle at the same depth in the lowermost mantle. These sluggish BMSs could be maintained for several hundreds of million of years (Supplementary Fig. 1). For comparison, we formulate an isochemical convection case to investigate the mobility of purely thermal LLSVPs2. A great subduction girdle akin to the Pacific ring of fire subduction girdle and plume bundles can be obtained with the same yield stress as the thermochemical convection models (Fig. 4a). We define plumes (purely thermal LLSVPs) as the areas of temperature higher than Tp(z) (see “methods”), and find the horizontal velocity of plumes is similar to that of the bulk mantle in the lower mantle (Fig. 4b). Thus, comparing Figs. 4, 3, the mobility of purely thermal LLSVPs is higher than thermochemical LLSVPs.

To further clarify such mobility contrast, we calculate the vote maps (Methods) of BMSs and plumes for the preferred thermal and thermochemical models over the last 630 Myrs (Fig. 5). The main parts of the BMSs at the bottom of the mantle remain stable during this period of time, while the margins of BMSs are deformed and migrate depending on the push from the sinking slabs (column 1 of Fig. 5a, b), which is consistent with the temporal evolution of the BMSs (Supplementary Fig. 2). In contrast, plumes in the deep mantle of the thermal model are so mobile that almost none of them can be maintained for such a period of time compared to the BMSs in the thermochemical model (Column 3 of Fig. 5a, b). Our vote maps, therefore, indicate that the thermochemical LLSVPs in the lower mantle are more sluggish in their lateral motion than thermal LLSVPs (Fig. 5a, b). These differences between the thermal and thermochemical models in the deep mantle may also affect the temporal and spatial distributions of plumes in the shallow mantle. Since the roots of these plumes are generally associated with the hot basal mantle structures, the plumes in the shallow mantle are temporally less intermittent and spatially more stationary in the thermochemical model than those in the thermal model (columns 2 and 4 of Fig. 5a, b).

Influence of physical properties of basal mantle structures on model space
The topology of BMSs in our models (i.e., 1, 2, or no piles) is affected by the distribution of the subduction girdle (Fig. 1). However, in turn, the pattern of BMSs may also affect the plate tectonic configuration. We thus adjust the buoyancy ratio, which previous work has shown to be the first-order factor dominating the configuration of BMSs12,18,23 regardless of the vigor of mantle convection to change the pattern of BMSs. We vary the buoyancy ratio (B) from 0.18–0.30, corresponding to the chemical density contrast from 74–124 kg/m3 (Supplementary Fig. 3), which is consistent with the estimate of density anomalies in the lower mantle4, and keep yield stress and chemical viscosity contrast constant (100 MPa and 10, respectively). We find the BMSs are fully entrained by ambient mantle materials, and subduction forms a great-circle girdle in small buoyancy ratio cases (B = 0.18 and 0.20). In large buoyancy ratio cases (B = 0.22, 0.26, and 0.30), subduction also forms a great-circle girdle, but BMSs form in 2 piles with different topographies and shapes. Thus, the adjustment of the buoyancy ratio in large buoyancy ratio cases has effects on the topography of BMSs but limited effects on the position of subduction zones, hence the plate tectonic configuration, and the stability of BMSs (Supplementary Figs. 3, 4).

Tomography study indicates that LLSVPs contain more bridgmanite than the ambient mantle4. MgSiO3 bridgmanite is more viscous than MgO periclase by up to 1000 times24,25. A chemical viscosity contrast of 10 for BMSs in our preferred model can decrease the viscosity difference between BMSs and the ambient mantle because the BMSs are hot and thermally less viscous26. We vary the chemical viscosity contrasts between the BMSs and the ambient mantle from 1–100 to test the influence of chemical viscosity on the pattern of BMSs (Supplementary Fig. 5). With increasing chemical viscosity contrast, the topography of BMSs rises, and the area of BMSs decreases, due to the decreasing efficiency of mantle convection and hence decreasing heat loss efficiency26. When the chemical viscosity contrast is >30, BMSs form three piles, and the position of subduction changes considerably. BMSs form two piles when the chemical viscosity contrast is <30. Note that the horizontal velocity of BMSs in these cases remains notably slower than that of the bulk mantle, indicating these BMSs are relatively sluggish (Supplementary Fig. 6).
paper_content.methods:
Thermochemical mantle convection models
We assume an anelastic and compressible fluid with an infinite Prandtl number, and we solve the non-dimensional equations of mass, momentum, heat, and chemical conservation in a 3D spherical shell on the Yin-Yang grid40 using the finite difference/volume code StagYY17. The main model setup used here is similar to that published previously18, and we further take plastic yielding into account to generate plate boundaries19,20. The reference Rayleigh number Ras is expressed as:

Ras = \rho s g\alpha \eta s \Delta T s D3 / \kappa 0 s, (1)

where \rho s is the surface density, g the gravity, \alpha the thermal expansion, \eta s the surface viscosity and \kappa 0 s the surface thermal diffusivity. In this study, Ras is fixed to 1 \times 108.

Temperature-, depth-, and composition-dependent viscosity coupled with plastic yielding is used. Meanwhile, we imposed a viscosity jump of 30 at 660 km depth. The viscosity is described fully by

\eta eff = 1 / (1/\eta(T,d,C) + 1/\eta Y), (2)

with

\eta(T,d,C) = \eta 0 (1+29H(d-660)) exp(VaD) exp(EaT+T off / (T+T s)) + KaC, (3)

and

\eta Y = (\sigma 0 + \sigma_ z) / 2\epsilon_ \Pi, (4)

where \eta Y is the yield viscosity, \sigma 0 the surface yield stress, \sigma_ z the yield stress gradient, which is set to 0 to introduce transform faults as suggested by previous study41, and \epsilon_ \Pi the second invariant of the strain rate tensor. H is the Heaviside step function, Va the non-dimensional activation volume, Ea the non-dimensional activation energy, T off the offset temperature, which is fixed to 0.88\Delta T s to reduce the temperature-induced viscosity variation at the surface, C the composition field, and Ka the parameter controlling the chemical viscosity contrast \Delta \eta C = exp(Ka). No prescribed plate boundaries are imposed and the yield stress help to generate plate-like behavior at the top of the domain. To avoid numerical problems, the viscosity is truncated between 10-3 and 105 of the reference viscosity.

Initial condition and model setup
To introduce basal mantle structures (BMSs), we initially setup an even dense layer above CMB whose thickness is 0.06 (173 km in dimensional unit)42,43. The grid resolution is 64 \times 192 \times 64 \times 2 with grid refinement at both the surface, the bottom, and at 660 km depth (the ringwoodite phase change to bridgmanite). The boundary conditions of the bottom and the top are free-slip, and the temperature of the top is set to 0.12 (300 K), and the bottom is 1.5 (3750 K) (Supplementary Fig. 8a). The model includes both internal and basal heating. The internal heating rate is 7.08 \times 10-12 W/kg, as suggested in ref. 44. Given the LLSVPs possibly enriched in heat-producing elements, we assume the heating rate of the BMS is ~7 times that of the ambient mantle materials26,45. The superadiabatic thermal boundary layers are located at the surface and the bottom, the thickness of which is ~87 km. Random temperature perturbation is implemented at both boundaries. The curvature of the shell f defined as the ratio between the radius of the core and the total radius is set to 0.55 corresponding to the Earth’s value. We use a tracer ratio method to track the compositional field46. Two types of tracers are used to represent the compositional field, where 0 corresponds to the ambient mantle, and 1 corresponds to BMS material. The number of total tracers of all models is 24 million, corresponding to about 15 tracers per cell, which is sufficient for simulating material entrainment46. The composition field is calculated from the ratio between BMS tracers and total tracers. The initial thickness of the BMS material is 0.06 (corresponding to 173 km), and the initial volume of the BMS material is ~3% of the mantle42,43. The density contrast between BMSs and the ambient mantle is controlled by the buoyancy ratio

B = \alpha s \rho s \Delta T s / \Delta \rho c, (5)

where \Delta \rho c is the density contrast between BMSs and the ambient mantle.

Detection of plumes and slabs
To determine plumes and subduction zones in our models, we calculate threshold temperatures of plumes and slabs following those of ref. 47, which assumes that a point is located within a plume (subduction zone) if the temperature at this point is higher (lower) than:

T p(d) = T avg(d) + fp(T max(d) - T avg(d)), (6)

T s(d) = T avg(d) + fs(T min(d) - T avg(d)), (7)

where T avg(d), T max(d) and T min(d) are the horizontally averaged, maximum, and minimum temperature at depth d, and fp and fs are fixed to 0.5 and 0.1, respectively, in this study.

Horizontal velocities of BMSs and plumes
The horizontal velocities of BMSs and plumes are defined as the root-mean-square averaged velocity within the BMSs and plumes at each depth by

V HBMSs(d) = \sqrt{ (\int C>0.5 V H2 dA) / (\int C>0.5 dA) }, (8)

V HPlumes(d) = \sqrt{ (\int T>Tp(d) V H2 dA) / (\int T>Tp(d) dA) }, (9)

where V H = (V\theta, V\phi) is the horizontal velocity at the point of (d, \theta, \phi), \theta colatitude, \phi longitude, dA infinitesimal area. The temporal variation of the horizontal velocity of BMS is calculated at each timestep by

V HBMSs = \sqrt{ (\int C>0.5 V H2 dV) / (\int C>0.5 dV) }, (10)

where dV is infinitesimal volume.

Vote maps of BMSs and plumes
To quantify the stability of BMSs, we calculate vote maps of BMSs following a similar strategy of ref. 48. For a given depth of the composition field, a binary threshold of 0 (no BMSs) or 1 (BMSs) is applied to every latitude-longitude pixel in each time slice within the period of time we selected, followed by a pixel-wise summation of all N time slices within the period selected. The pixels of the vote map hence take values between 0 and N. We then divided the value of each pixel on the vote map by N to get a normalized vote map on which all pixels take values between 0 and 1. A value of 0 on a vote map indicates no BMSs have existed in this pixel during the whole selected period of time, while a value of 1 indicates that BMSs have existed in this pixel at some point during the whole selected period of time, and a value between 0 and 1 indicates the normalized time length that BMSs have existed in this pixel compared to the selected period of time. Vote maps of plumes are calculated by using the same method in the temperature field.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
Review of Sluggish basal mantle structures support their long-lived stability, submitted to Nature
Communications by Shi et al. 2023
The two antipodal tomographically-observed large low-shear velocity provinces (LLSVPs) are the most
distinct structures in Earth's interior. Although they could still be purely thermal, most of the community
explain them as intrinsically dense materials that has higher density than the background mantle. Given
this assumption and also based on paleomagnetic results from large igneous provinces, hotspots and
kimberlites, it has been hypothesized that the LLSVPs may be temporally stationary over hundreds of
millions of years. But a stable LLSVPs is hard to reconcile with many observations and models, which
reveals the mobile subduction zone and passive and deforming patterns of LLSVPs. Thus whether LLSVPs
remain stable or dynamic is one unsolved question in Earth's interior community.
In this manuscript, the authors performed global mantle convection simulations to assess whether the
two LLSVPs were stationary over relatively short geological time scales. They found that the average
horizontal velocity of the thermochemical piles (LLSVPs in models) in their preferred Earth-like models is
~4 times slower than the background mantle, indicating the LLSVPs can be stationary over 200-300 Myr
to allow the connection of surface volcanisms to the deep mantle structure as indicated by geological
evidence. I commend the authors for a clear written and distinct approach to understand the mobility of
LLSVPs–which is one of the hottest debates on LLSVPs, and for undertaking global 3D models which is
computationally expensive. However, I find that the calculations are not appropriate for supporting their
conclusion. Some nontrivial issues are ignored, which would greatly change the results.
First, one of the most critical issues is their models did not include plate reconstruction history, which is
essential in the validation of numerical models and a key and necessary component in related studies for
decades (e.g., Hans-Peter Bunge et al., 2002). Including realistic surface plate motions is crucial as
indicated by two very recent papers, one in nature (Flament et al., 2022) and another one in nature
geoscience (Bodur and Flament, 2023). These two studies clearly show that the mobile LLSVPs can
statistically explain associated large igneous provinces and kimberlite eruptions at the surface for the
past 320 Myr, without a need for stationary LLSVPs. Although the authors’ models with reasonable
lithosphere yield stress can form two antipodal LLSVPs dividing by the Pacific-like girdle, similar results
have been already shown more than 15 years ago (McNamara & Zhong, 2005, Nature). The previous
study further made a detailed comparison of their geodynamic calculation and tomography models,
which is important to validate numerical models, and this comparison also was not considered in the
study.
Another major comment is a technical problem: whether it is useful to compare the average velocity of
LLSVPs with that of the ambient mantle. It is well known that the surface and upper mantle have higher
velocity compared to the lower mantle, where the two LLSVP reside. Thus, without any experiments, I
expect to see a lower velocity of LLSVPs compared to the average velocity of the bulk mantle. This
actually can be clearly seen in their figure 3. It might be helpful to compare the LLSVP velocity with the
ambient mantle only in the lower mantle, but from their figure the average velocity between them is
similar (0.3 vs 1 cm/year). I appreciate the authors presented another isothermal calculation that shows
a purely thermal LLSVP have a similar average velocity to the bulk mantle, but how the results will
change if you use a different threshold of defining the plumes? A short summary for this comment is that
I think it is much more meaningful to explore the average lateral motion of plumes from LLSVPs, rather
than the horizontal velocity of LLSVPs themselves, to help constrain the mobility vs fixity of LLSVPs.
When exploring the velocity of LLSVPs, the viscosity is one of the most critical parameters. This study
only considered cases where LLSVPs are of higher chemical viscosity contrast (1–100 times) given one
study suggesting it may include more bridgmanite than the ambient mantle. However, we have to admit
that the viscosity of LLSVPs are still highly uncertain. Because it is widely accepted they are hotter than
the ambient mantle, you might want to explore cases with a lower chemical viscosity contrast, such as
0.01. For a lower viscosity of LLSVPs, I expect the average velocity would be similar or even faster than
that of the average lower mantle.
Another specific comment is I am a bit concern of the time scale in your reference 3D model. It feels like
the whole simulation is modelled for only a few hundred million year, rather than 4.5 Gyr. I am not a user
for StagYY, but I suggest doubling check the time scale during dimensionalization. The time scale in other
3D StayYY models looks more realistic and dynamic. If there is not an issue, it may be related to the
rheology structures or initial conditions. In terms of visualizations, the plume structures in your uploaded
video seems too massive, even bigger than the downwelling structures. This is in contrast with many
numerical models (they also used plasticity), and using a different threshold for both slabs and plumes
may help.
Given these, I cannot recommend publication of the manuscript in its current form. Despite my non-
supportive review, I’d like to make the positive note that I believe the motivation of this study is very well
selected. I encourage them to find a way to bring more appropriate dynamic models, particularly with
plate reconstruction history (now the past 1Ga history is available at Müller et al., 2022), and improved
algorithm to address this problem.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
LLSVPs probably represent a combination of primordial Fe-rich material and dense recycled oceanic
crust, and exploring their potential stability over hundreds of million years is of vital importance of
understanding the workings of our planet. Testing their stability by numerical modelling is highly
dependent on parameterization and I welcome this study that explore their stability under different
parameter space. I am not an expert on StagYY modelling but I find their parameterization and
conclusions to be very sound. The paper is well written, the rationale is very clear, it is well referenced
and I truly enjoyed reading this paper.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
This article presents numerical models of mantle convection to examine the stability and longevity of
basal mantle structures (BMSs) which serve as a proxy for LLSVPs in the real Earth. This could be an
exciting result if additional evidence can be provided to support claims made in the paper.
The authors run a series of models with various parameters to determine the longevity of the BMSs.
However, more evidence is needed to justify their claim of BMS stability over hundreds of millions of
years. As presented, the work is not so convincing. There are some modeling details which should be
specified to further understand the model setup. There are also some grammatical and style issues
which could be fixed to enhance readability.
The authors show that 2 piles can be formed at the CMB with various parameters. However, there should
be more convincing evidence that these results show longevity or stability of these BMSs.
The authors claim that the velocity in the BMSs is lower than the ambient mantle and surface plate
velocities. However, the authors did not show that this lower velocity is consistent over any length of
time. The velocity measured in the BMSs could be a measure the internal convection rate (see >>>>) and
not a measure of how the BMS are moving across the CMB. The paper does not provide convincing
enough evidence that the velocities measured reflect the stability of the BMSs. The authors should
explain in more detail how the velocity is being calculated. It would be helpful to include a plot of how
the velocities are changing over time since that would be a better indication of pile stability.
The authors should show snapshots of a model with degree-2 structure at various times to show the
stability of the BMSs. It is difficult to tell exactly from video how long the 2 piles are lasting in the same
place at CMB.
There are many model details that are missing or poorly described to be able to be confident in the
results as presented. The models are described as similar to previous research but what exactly does this
mean? Are the model parameters the same? the resolution? Are the plate boundaries prescribed in the
model and then plastic yielding allows for subduction ? How are the boundaries determined? What is
the viscosity profile in the model that would allow for slabs to easily penetrate into the lower mantle and
push aside the BMSs. Are all models run for the same dimensional time?
The authors quantify the mobility of the BMSs by calculating the horizontal velocities of the BMSs (is that
velocity inside the BMS or their edge motion as whole pile?). They compare these with a purely thermal
model. They compare the motion of thermal plumes to the ambient mantle but previous work has
shown plumes to be influenced by mantle motion. A better comparison would be thermo plume to
thermochemical plumes rather than the plumes to piles. Or more description is needed to justify how
thermo plume to thermochemical pile comparisons support stability.
Figure images are clear but captions and divisions could be made more clear. In particular there are
multiple references to Figure 1d but there is no "d" labelled on figure 1. In fact Figures 1, S1, S2 are all in
columns and should referenced as such in the paper (or labeled with a, b, c, etc).

In this manuscript, the authors performed global mantle convection simulations to assess whether
the two LLSVPs were stationary over relatively short geological time scales. They found that the
average horizontal velocity of the thermochemical piles (LLSVPs in models) in their preferred
Earth-like models is ~4 times slower than the background mantle, indicating the LLSVPs can be
stationary over 200-300 Myr to allow the connection of surface volcanisms to the deep mantle
structure as indicated by geological evidence. I commend the authors for a clear written and distinct
approach to understand the mobility of LLSVPs–which is one of the hottest debates on LLSVPs,
and for undertaking global 3D models which is computationally expensive. However, I find that
the calculations are not appropriate for supporting their conclusion. Some nontrivial issues are
ignored, which would greatly change the results.
Response: Thank you for acknowledging the potential significance of our study and for the
constructive suggestions and comments that helped us to improve the manuscript. Below are our
point-by-point responses to your suggestions and comments.
1) First, one of the most critical issues is their models did not include plate reconstruction history,
which is essential in the validation of numerical models and a key and necessary component in
related studies for decades (e.g., Hans-Peter Bunge et al., 2002). Including realistic surface plate
motions is crucial as indicated by two very recent papers, one in nature (Flament et al., 2022) and
another one in nature geoscience (Bodur and Flament, 2023). These two studies clearly show that
the mobile LLSVPs can statistically explain associated large igneous provinces and kimberlite
eruptions at the surface for the past 320 Myr, without a need for stationary LLSVPs. Although the
authors’ models with reasonable lithosphere yield stress can form two antipodal LLSVPs divided
by the Pacific-like girdle, similar results have been already shown more than 15 years ago
(McNamara & Zhong, 2005, Nature). The previous study further made a detailed comparison of
their geodynamic calculation and tomography models, which is important to validate numerical
models, and this comparison also was not considered in the study.
Response: We thank the reviewer for expanding our perspective and for reminding us of another
advanced simulation strategy for surface conditions. This question deserves careful clarification.
The reviewer is correct in that plate reconstructions are important for validating the style of mantle
convection, including the work presented in this study. Here, we want to clarify that the conclusion
of our study—the long-term stability of LLSVPs with a suitable lithospheric yield stress—is not
inconsistent with our knowledge of ancient plate reconstructions. For example, the 200–300 Myr
stability of our modeled LLSVPs is similar to results directly based on plate reconstructions
(McNamara & Zhong, 2005). We hope to emphasize that the LLSVPs in our models are not
entirely fixed as one may envisage from some end-member models (e.g., Torsvik et al., 2010).
Instead, we showed that the bulk LLSVPs are largely stationary, but their edges are deforming and
migrating depending on the push of the sinking slabs. This is also what Flament et al. (2022)
demonstrated in their model. Another independent verification from plate reconstructions comes
from the study of Conrad et al. (2013) where they found that global plate motions obeyed a
stationary degree-2 pattern during the past ~250 Myr.
[Figure Redacted]
On the other hand, we also want to make it clear that models with imposed plate kinematics at the
surface cannot objectively conclude on the stability of deep mantle structures like LLSVPs, due to
the forced nature of the surface boundary conditions. In contrast, a freely moving surface like the
one incorporated in our models is more appropriate, as demonstrated in earlier studies (e.g., Zhong
et al., 2007). Because of this philosophy, the cited works by the reviewer (e.g., McNamara &
Zhong, 2005; Flament et al., 2022) cannot be used to claim the true stability of the LLSVPs, as
they all depend on the style of the imposed plate motions. The fact that our result resembles theirs
reveals that the reconstructed plate motion since as early as 250 Ma is likely reasonable, which is,
again, consistent with the finding of Conrad et al. (2013).
This brings up another question regarding the pre-250 Ma plate reconstruction: should one trust
the recent plate reconstructions managed to extend beyond the supercontinent Pangea or fully
dynamic simulations like the ones we propose here? Many people realize that these plate
reconstructions were done with limited constraints, especially from the ocean basins which are the
key constraints for the reconstructions for the past 250 Myrs reconstructions. Indeed, the
reconstruction experts themselves clearly warned about this caveat (e.g., Müller et al., 2022) by
stating that these early reconstructions enforced a constant mean global plate motion over time
such that oceanic subduction never stopped, even after the assembly of a supercontinent;
consequently, published plate reconstructions all feature a dominant degree-2 pattern over time,
with a circum- supercontinent subduction girdle reminiscent of the degree-2 convection pattern
first proposed in Zhong et al. (2007). No matter if this assumption is valid or not, such a long-term
degree-2 pattern is again similar to our finding of LLSVPs stability for up to 600 Myr. We therefore
conclude that our result is consistent with and supported by approaches using plate reconstructions,
and that our approach is more appropriate for examining the long-term stability of LLSVPs than
those with imposed plate motions—or at least provides a viable alternative approach.
2) Another major comment is a technical problem: whether it is useful to compare the average
velocity of LLSVPs with that of the ambient mantle. It is well known that the surface and upper
mantle have higher velocity compared to the lower mantle, where the two LLSVP reside. Thus,
without any experiments, I expect to see a lower velocity of LLSVPs compared to the average
velocity of the bulk mantle. This actually can be clearly seen in their figure 3. It might be helpful
to compare the LLSVP velocity with the ambient mantle only in the lower mantle, but from their
figure the average velocity between them is similar (0.3 vs 1 cm/year). I appreciate the authors
presented another isothermal calculation that shows a purely thermal LLSVP have a similar
average velocity to the bulk mantle, but how the results will change if you use a different threshold
of defining the plumes? A short summary for this comment is that I think it is much more
meaningful to explore the average lateral motion of plumes from LLSVPs, rather than the
horizontal velocity of LLSVPs themselves, to help constrain the mobility vs fixity of LLSVPs.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this comment. This comment deserves a detailed
clarification.
First, we agree with the reviewer that the surface and upper mantle have higher velocities compared
to the lower mantle. There might be some misunderstanding in comparing the velocities between
LLSVPs and the ambient mantle. In our study, we compared the averaged horizontal velocity
differences between LLSVPs and the bulk mantle at the same depth. We found that the
thermochemical LLSVPs have a lower velocity of about 1/4 that of the bulk mantle as shown in
Figure 3 (0.3 vs ~1.2 cm/y), meanwhile, pure thermal LLSVPs have a similar velocity compared
to the bulk mantle as shown in Figure 4 (~1.4 vs ~1.5 cm/y). This difference between thermal and
thermochemical LLSVPs suggests that thermochemical LLSVPs are sluggish structures in the
lower mantle. We have clarified the comparison at the same depth in the revised manuscript (line
95) and removed the comparison with surface velocity to avoid misunderstanding (line 95).
Second, we thank the reviewer for the suggestion to test “a different threshold of defining the
plume”. We tested different thresholds (0.4, 0.5, and 0.6) to define plumes (Fig. R2), and we found
that although the structure of plumes becomes less broad with increasing threshold, the averaged
horizontal velocities of plumes are comparable to each other, and no significant differences were
caused by changing the threshold. And this observation also applies to the thermochemical plumes.
Following the reviewer’s suggestion, we use a threshold of 0.5 in the revision (instead of 0.4 in
the original manuscript) to improve the visualization of our results.

Third, we appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion to explore the average lateral motion of plumes.
Because an individual plume has a much shorter life cycle compared to the length of time in our
study and is therefore not easy to track, we have made new calculations to plot the vote maps (see
Methods) of plumes as well as that of the thermochemical LLSVPs for the reference case and the
thermal convection case to show how the locations of these features change with time (Fig. 5) in
the last 630 Myrs of evolution. We can observe that the main parts of the LLSVPs at the bottom
of the mantle remain stationary during this period of time, while the margins are deforming and
migrating with time depending on the push of the sinking slabs. We also plot the vote maps of
plumes at 300 km, and consistent with our main conclusion, the plumes in the thermochemical
case are more stationary compared to those in the thermal convection model (Fig. 5, columns 2
and 3). The vote maps also indicate that the thermochemical piles in the lower mantle are sluggish
in their lateral motion compared to the plumes above them, which again can serve as one line of
evidence to support our main conclusion that these BMSs are sluggish structures in the lower
mantle. We have added the description of the features mentioned above in the revised manuscript
(lines 105-113).
3) When exploring the velocity of LLSVPs, the viscosity is one of the most critical parameters.
This study only considered cases where LLSVPs are of higher chemical viscosity contrast (1–100
times) given one study suggesting it may include more bridgmanite than the ambient mantle.
However, we have to admit that the viscosity of LLSVPs are still highly uncertain. Because it is
widely accepted they are hotter than the ambient mantle, you might want to explore cases with a
lower chemical viscosity contrast, such as 0.01. For a lower viscosity of LLSVPs, I expect the
average velocity would be similar or even faster than that of the average lower mantle.
Response: The viscosity of LLSVPs is affected by both temperature and composition, as we
detailed in the Methods. Since LLSVPs are hotter than the ambient mantle, the thermal viscosity
is smaller than for the ambient mantle, and for the case where chemical viscosity contrast equals
1, LLSVPs are already less viscous than the ambient mantle, as shown below (Fig. R3).

Less viscous LLSVPs lead to more mixing with the ambient mantle. If we further decrease the
chemical viscosity contrast to 0.1(i.e., by one order of magnitude), the stable part of LLSVP
decreases, nonetheless overall, the velocity of the stable part remains smaller than that of the bulk
mantle (Fig. R4). The primordial piles cannot be preserved during the entire run if the chemical
viscosity contrast decreases to 0.01(i.e., an additional order of magnitude). To summarize, the
chemically distinct LLSVPs cannot preserve in the lower mantle during the entire run if their
chemical viscosity contrast is relatively small (e.g., 0.01); and the velocity of stable LLSVPs can
be still smaller than that of the bulk mantle even if the overall viscosity is smaller than the bulk
mantle.

Given these, I cannot recommend publication of the manuscript in its current form. Despite my

reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
See comments in attached Word document.
Comments to Author
The composition of the two continent-sized large low velocity provinces (LLVPs), that are consistently
imaged by seismic tomographic inversions atop the core-mantle boundary, has been a topic of debate
since their discovery four decades ago. This study aims to address this controversy using a suite of
billion-year-duration global mantle convection models that include plastic yielding to reproduce plate-
like behaviour. The authors find that forming two antipodal LLVPs (or Basal Mantle Structures [BMSs])
at the present-day requires intermediate values of mantle yield strength (~100 MPa), as well as denser
and (~+100 kg m-3) and slightly more viscous material within the BMSs. The result is that the BMSs
move a factor of ~4 slower than their surroundings, producing relative stability over 100-Myr
timescales.
I am evaluating this paper after it has already undergone a thorough review, with specific instructions
to comment on the degree to which the main concerns raised by Reviewers 1 and 3 have been
resolved (i.e., the suggested need to use plate reconstructions to set surface boundary conditions and
the level of support given for the main conclusions regarding LLVP mobility). The authors have
substantially revised and augmented their manuscript and overall, I think they have carefully
considered and more than adequately addressed these key criticisms (see below), as well as the
reviewers’ other concerns. In my view, this is an interesting piece of work that provides further
independent evidence to support the view that LLVPs are chemically distinct from the ambient mantle
and move more sluggishly. I have some relatively minor additional concerns and suggestions I would
like the authors to address, but I would be happy to see this manuscript published in once these are
dealt with.
Comments on Response to Key Concerns Raised in Previous Reviews
1) Suggested need to use plate reconstructions as a surface boundary condition (Reviewer 1)
I disagree with Reviewer 1’s contention that adopting a plate-reconstruction-based approach is
“crucial” to addressing the question of LLVP stability in general. I would agree with them if the authors
were aiming to accurately reconstruct LLVP motion over the past 200-300 Myrs and link it directly to
the geological record. However, this work—as I read it—aims only to place bounds on the length of
time over which a degree-two LLVP structure, like that presently observed, can remain relatively
stationary. That is, they are testing whether relative stationarity over a ~250 Myr period (as advocated
by some) is possible given the geodynamic conditions required to form such structures in the first
place, not whether such limited lateral movement actually occurred in the last 250 Ma of Earth history.
I therefore agree with the authors that their work provides a useful counterpoint to previous plate
reconstruction-based approaches for investigating LLVP mobility. As highlighted by the authors in their
rebuttal, the application of plate reconstructions also has its downsides, since reconstructions are
likely to be highly inaccurate prior to ~150 Ma due to a lack of oceanic constraints and, even at younger
ages, imposed surface forcing may not be dynamically consistent with the underlying flow field,
introducing artefacts. Both methods (fully dynamic and plate-reconstruction-based) have their
advantages and shortcomings, but when simulating LLVP formation and mobility on very long
timescales (>250 Ma)—as is the focus here—it is reasonable to argue that the fully dynamic approach
may give comparably reliable results. In any case, their results are broadly compatible with certain of
those obtained from plate-reconstruction-based techniques, with substantial, albeit slow, reshaping
of LLVPs over time (see changes in BMS location in Figure S5 and variation in the dominant degree of
the lower mantle temperature power spectrum in Figure S7).
2) Disputed level of support for the conclusions regarding LLVP mobility (Reviewers 1 & 3)
Reviewer 1’s other qualms about the level of support for the conclusions are, I think, mainly the result
of certain misunderstandings. These have now been clarified by the authors, and I feel that these
previous misgivings have now been demonstrated to be unfounded. First, the authors have always
been comparing LLVP and ambient mantle velocities at the same depth (i.e., not comparing bulk values
for the whole mantle). Secondly, cases where LLVP viscosity is lower than that of the ambient mantle
have already been tested by the authors, since the high temperatures obtained in these regions,
coupled with strongly temperature-dependent viscosity, outweighs the effect of the imposed
chemical viscosity contrast when it is set to low values. Finally, there appear to be no problems with
the dimensionalisation of the calculations, and the choice of threshold for identifying plumes is shown
to have negligible impact on the conclusions.
Reviewer 3’s comments centre on the degree to which LLVPs (or BMSs) have been demonstrated to
remain relatively stationary over 100-Myr periods. In response, the authors have added much needed
methodological detail regarding how horizontal velocities inside the BMSs are calculated, as well as
several new figures to support their interpretation (e.g., Figure 5). Overall, these clearly show that,
while their margins deform, the bulk of the modelled BMSs move relatively little over a 630 Myr
period, addressing Reviewer 3’s point. That said, I do have some queries regarding the vote maps used
to conduct the thermal versus thermochemical plume mobility comparison (see below).
Further Comments
1) Figure 1: What time in the model run is plotted here? The final timestep in each case? Are they
random snapshots (and if so, how are they chosen)? This information should be made clear in the
caption.
2) Figure 2: What time in the model run is plotted here? Or is the area of BMS and 1 pile/2 pile
categorisation being calculated based on average behaviour? This information needs to be made
clear in the caption.
3) Figure 5: In the thermal and thermochemical plume vote map comparison in the last two columns
of this figure (maps and histograms), it appears as if there is a larger overall proportion of plumes
through time in the thermochemical case; i.e., if you integrated the voting values over the surface
of the 300 km depth slice in each case it does not look like they would give the same total, a
conclusion which seems to be confirmed by the area under the histograms being different. It is
also not clear to me, even after accounting for the apparently smaller number of plumes present
over the 630 Myr time period, that those in the thermal models are more laterally mobile than
their thermochemical counterparts. Instead, it looks like regions with non-zero plume voting
values are distributed over a smaller area in the thermal case, and that the lower maximum voting
values (generally <0.2) are a result of individual plumes being shorter-lived rather than more
laterally mobile.
Could it be that the apparently larger time-integrated proportion and greater spatial coverage of
plumes in the thermochemical models is simply an illusion caused by the adopted colour scheme
and histogram y-axis? What I mean is, could it be that thermal plumes are so mobile that many
pixels have voting values that are non-zero yet so small that the adopted colourbar makes them
appear as if they are equal to zero? If that is the case, the vote map colourbar should be modified
to differentiate between a voting value of zero (i.e., plume not present at a given location at any
time in the 630 Myr model time period) and a very small value (plume locally present for at least
one time step). In this case, the y-axis range on the relevant histogram would also need to be
extended to highlight the larger number of near-zero values in the thermal case and to
demonstrate that the area under the histogram remains the same as that in the
thermochemical case, despite the distribution being more positively skewed.
If there really is a greater proportion of plume material through time in the thermochemical
models, then this result requires some explanation, especially given that the definition applied
here uses a relative rather than absolute plume temperature threshold. As a result, despite the
extra radiogenic heating from the BMSs (~7 times ambient) in the thermochemical models, it’s
not clear that there should be a greater number of features classified as plumes since higher
average temperatures due to elevated radiogenic heating values won’t inherently lead to more
plume material. Similarly, if the white regions in the vote maps really do have voting values equal
to zero then, as stated above, it looks to me like there are fewer non-zero values in the
thermochemical case, indicating that these plumes are potentially more laterally mobile, not less.
That said, the higher maximum voting values do suggest that individual plumes are less
intermittent in the thermochemical case, which if confirmed, is an interesting result.
If the apparently smaller time-integrated proportion of plumes in the thermal model is a real
feature, then a physical explanation should be given, and it should be clarified that rather than
necessarily being less laterally mobile, the thermochemical model plumes are longer-lived. To
determine relative lateral mobility, average horizontal velocity of the plume regions over time
needs to be assessed instead. Alternatively, if the apparently smaller time-integrated proportion
of plumes it is a plotting artefact, then this issue should be rectified through modification of the
map colourbar and histogram y-axis, as suggested above.
4) Line 31: I would suggest adding references to Lu et al., 2020, G-Cubed and/or Richards et al.,
2023, EPSL here, as these studies recently showed that LLVPs are not purely thermal (i.e., their
basal portions are chemically anomalous) whilst reconciling a wider range of geophysical
constraints than the currently cited papers, making them more convincing in my view. That said,
I must declare a potential bias/conflict here as I am an author of one of the suggested papers.
5) Lines 75-76: Do you mean “can maintain degree-2 structure for about 630 Myr” or “can maintain
degree-2 structure for up to 630 Myr”? It’s not clear to me whether the focus here is on the
maximum length of time for which piles are stable or the average length of time. Both would be
helpful to state somewhere.
6) Lines 88–90: Check grammar and sentence construction, currently very hard to parse this
sentence.
7) Lines 111–113: I don’t see how the referenced vote maps (Figure 5) confirm that thermochemical
LLVPs move more sluggishly than thermal LLVPs since thermal LLVPs are not plotted, only thermal
plumes at 300 km depth. This sentence should either be removed or better justified (e.g., by
showing the plume vote map at 2800 km depth to illustrate mobility of the thermal LLVP over
last 630 Myrs of the model run).
8) Paragraph starting on Line 115: You should mention somewhere in this paragraph that yield
stress and chemical viscosity contrast are being held constant (100 MPa and 10) in these variable
buoyancy number runs.
9) Lines 133–135: I don’t fully understand why the increases in BMS topography and decreases in
BMS area that occur for large chemical viscosity contrasts are the result of decreasing heat loss
efficiency. Can this argument be fleshed out a little more?
10) Line 154–155: Not clear what kind of “end-member” these models are argued to represent from
a yield stress point of view, i.e., are they a low-strength or high-strength end-member? They have
low yield stress compared to some estimates for anhydrous oceanic lithosphere, but high yield
stress compared to others (e.g., estimates for continental lithosphere and oceanic lithosphere at
plate boundaries), so it is not clear which extreme is being argued for here. Can this point be
clarified?
11) Line 177–179: Not clear how the vote maps show that it’s easier for slabs to move the slab
graveyard surrounding the BMSs rather than the BMSs themselves. This point was picked up on
by Reviewer 1 too. Comparisons of the horizontal velocity of the slabs in the lower mantle
compared to those of the BMSs would help to substantiate this claim.
12) Lines 184–187: I don’t really follow the argument that “the present antipodal LLSVPs should have
been cut by a subduction girdle one time from the age of their formation more easily than there
after”. Why does the ease with which LLVPs can be cut by a subduction girdle change over time?
13) Lines 187–189: Struggling to understand what is being proposed in this sentence and how it links
with the previous one. Is the idea that the girdle cuts a single BMS into two and these two BMSs
are then shifted to their present antipodal configuration by continued slab push over the course
of a supercontinent cycle? Or is the argument that two distinct BMSs exist prior to girdle
formation but are not pushed into their present configuration until they interact with it? This
sentence could do with rewording to clarify these points.
14) Line 189–191: Ending the paper with these unresolved issues seems a slightly negative way to
finish. I would suggest concluding by reiterating what has been firmly established by this study
and its implications after the need for further study to resolve these open questions has been
outlined.
15) Line 224: Why is 173 km set for the initial BMS layer thickness? This value stands out as being
surprisingly specific so a short justification would help here. I assume this choice is related to the
3% volume fraction being assumed (Line 239), but even so, some reasoning should be given for
why these numbers are adopted.
16) Worth asking a mother-tongue English speaker to do a final language check. I found nothing that
affected my comprehension of the text (beyond the sentences specifically highlighted above),

boundaries are imposed…” or “No plate boundaries are prescribed…” in lines 217–218).

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Large low shear-wave velocity provinces (LLSVPs) in the lowermost mantle are the largest geological structures on Earth, but their origin and age remain highly enigmatic. Geological constraints suggest the stability of the LLSVPs since at least 200 million years ago. Here, we conduct numerical modeling of mantle convection with plate-like behavior that yields a Pacific-like girdle of mantle downwelling which successfully forms two antipodal basal mantle structures similar to the LLSVPs. Our parameterized results optimized to reflect LLSVP features exhibit velocities for the basal mantle structures that are ~4 times slower than the ambient mantle if they are thermochemical, while the velocity is similar to the ambient mantle if purely thermal. The sluggish motion of the thermochemical basal mantle structures in our models permits the notion that geological data from hundreds of millions of years ago are related to modern LLSVPs as they are essentially stationary over such time scales.

---

## Introduction

The makeup and origins of Earth’s deep and inaccessible interior have long been mysterious. Ever since the detection by seismic tomography of the two antipodal large low shear-wave velocity provinces (LLSVPs) — regions in the lowermost mantle in which the shear-wave velocity is lower than that of the ambient mantle1 — their origin has been extensively debated. Although a purely thermal origin of LLSVPs cannot be excluded2, multiple sources of geophysical data indicate that the LLSVPs are thermally hot and should also be chemically distinct3–6. Whether the LLSVPs derive most or part of their density from a primordial layer of dense materials (such as from the crystallization of magma ocean7 or moon-forming giant impact8) and/or a layer of subducted oceanic crust growing over time, the antiquity of their current morphology into two piles most likely developed at some later point in Earth’s history1. Yet despite great advances in recent decades, many features of the LLSVPs remain enigmatic. There is a great debate about the stability and antiquity of the LLSVPs. In general, there are two end-member interpretations where the LLSVPs are fixed, ancient structures9,10 or dynamic, young structures11–13.

Various types of geological data appear to suggest the African LLSVP has been essentially fixed since 200–300 million years ago (Ma) (i.e., supercontinent Pangaea age), including large igneous provinces (LIPs)10, palaeogeography14, and net characteristics of plate motions15. Some studies have even argued for LLSVP stability back to >500 Ma or even since early in Earth’s history9,16. Alternatively, recent work has challenged LLSVP stability as far back as ca. 200–300 Ma Pangaea age. Numerical modeling of basal mantle structures (BMSs; referring to LLSVPs created in models) parameterized by plate kinematics and thus the mobility of subduction zones at the surface and slabs sinking into the mantle suggest that the lower mantle is more dynamic than previously considered12. Although BMSs are suggested to be very actively dynamic in recent studies, this conclusion is based on imposed plate reconstructions whose accuracy decreases back in time12. Therefore, a fully dynamic approach provides a viable alternative approach.

In this study, we conduct numerical modeling of BMSs to assess their mobility under self-consistent mantle convection with plate-like lithospheric behavior as the top boundary condition. We explore the parameter space that does or does not permit the creation of two antipodal BMSs akin to the areal extent of the LLSVPs. Those results that successfully satisfy such criteria are able to constrain the relative velocity of the BMSs and the ambient mantle, thereby testing the validity of LLSVP stability on 100 million years (Myr) and 1 billion years (Gyr) timescales as both have been proposed by competing models.

---

## Results

Role of plate tectonics in the topology of basal mantle structures
Three-dimensional thermochemical mantle convection models in spherical geometry on the Yin-Yang grid17,18 were conducted with plastic yielding to generate plate boundaries at the top19,20 and an initially even basal layer of dense materials in an attempt to generate BMSs over an evolutionary period of 4.56 Gyrs (comparable to the history of the Earth; “Methods”). As our goal is to investigate the stability time scale of LLSVPs, we first investigate the reaction of the topology of BMSs to plate tectonics by varying the strength of the oceanic lithosphere. We then analyze the mobility of BMSs in an Earth-like model where a Pacific-like subduction girdle and antipodal degree-2 BMSs form.

In our models, slabs penetrate into the lower mantle21 and push aside the BMSs. When plastic yielding is taken into account, two antipodal BMSs are split by a great subduction girdle (Fig. 1d), which is consistent with the present-day Earth where the two LLSVPs are separated by the Pacific “ring of fire” of subduction at the surface as well as with previous 3D models12,22. In 2D convection models with plastic yielding, two antipodal slabs could cut the layered BMSs and then push them into two piles22. In our work, we achieve a 3-D Earth-like model with quasi-stationary BMSs that maintain degree-2 structure for about 630 Myrs when yield stress is set to 100 MPa (Fig. 1d).

To evaluate the influence of plate tectonics on BMSs, we vary the yield stress, hence the strength of the oceanic lithosphere from 10–200 MPa, which controls the plate tectonics configuration20. Figure 1 shows snapshots of the surface viscosity, BMSs, plumes, and subduction. In our series of models, the observed planforms can be divided into four groups. (i) Ultra-low yield stress (30 MPa) yields four subduction systems that stir BMSs, and no piles are observed on the CMB. (ii) Low yield stress (50 MPa) yields a triple-junction-like subduction zone that is concentrated in a semi-sphere and cannot migrate because of the hindering of intense upwelling from the margin or interior of the one-pile BMS with high topography. (iii) Intermediate yield stress (70–100 MPa) yields more than one subduction girdle that cuts the BMSs and pushes them into two piles, where the distance between them increases with increasing yield stress. (iv) High yield stress (200 MPa) yields one circular pile that is pushed against by the downwelling. We further find that successful Earth-like models with two antipodal piles covering the CMB with areas of ~25% similar to LLSVPs occur in our study within a narrow range of moderate yield stress (90–100 MPa) (Fig. 2).

More sluggish thermochemical LLSVPs than thermal LLSVPs
To quantify the mobility of LLSVPs, we calculate the horizontal velocities of BMSs and the ambient mantle in our simulations (Fig. 3). The horizontal velocities of the BMSs are ~4 times slower than that of the ambient mantle at the same depth in the lowermost mantle. These sluggish BMSs could be maintained for several hundreds of million of years (Supplementary Fig. 1). For comparison, we formulate an isochemical convection case to investigate the mobility of purely thermal LLSVPs2. A great subduction girdle akin to the Pacific ring of fire subduction girdle and plume bundles can be obtained with the same yield stress as the thermochemical convection models (Fig. 4a). We define plumes (purely thermal LLSVPs) as the areas of temperature higher than Tp(z) (see “methods”), and find the horizontal velocity of plumes is similar to that of the bulk mantle in the lower mantle (Fig. 4b). Thus, comparing Figs. 4, 3, the mobility of purely thermal LLSVPs is higher than thermochemical LLSVPs.

To further clarify such mobility contrast, we calculate the vote maps (Methods) of BMSs and plumes for the preferred thermal and thermochemical models over the last 630 Myrs (Fig. 5). The main parts of the BMSs at the bottom of the mantle remain stable during this period of time, while the margins of BMSs are deformed and migrate depending on the push from the sinking slabs (column 1 of Fig. 5a, b), which is consistent with the temporal evolution of the BMSs (Supplementary Fig. 2). In contrast, plumes in the deep mantle of the thermal model are so mobile that almost none of them can be maintained for such a period of time compared to the BMSs in the thermochemical model (Column 3 of Fig. 5a, b). Our vote maps, therefore, indicate that the thermochemical LLSVPs in the lower mantle are more sluggish in their lateral motion than thermal LLSVPs (Fig. 5a, b). These differences between the thermal and thermochemical models in the deep mantle may also affect the temporal and spatial distributions of plumes in the shallow mantle. Since the roots of these plumes are generally associated with the hot basal mantle structures, the plumes in the shallow mantle are temporally less intermittent and spatially more stationary in the thermochemical model than those in the thermal model (columns 2 and 4 of Fig. 5a, b).

Influence of physical properties of basal mantle structures on model space
The topology of BMSs in our models (i.e., 1, 2, or no piles) is affected by the distribution of the subduction girdle (Fig. 1). However, in turn, the pattern of BMSs may also affect the plate tectonic configuration. We thus adjust the buoyancy ratio, which previous work has shown to be the first-order factor dominating the configuration of BMSs12,18,23 regardless of the vigor of mantle convection to change the pattern of BMSs. We vary the buoyancy ratio (B) from 0.18–0.30, corresponding to the chemical density contrast from 74–124 kg/m3 (Supplementary Fig. 3), which is consistent with the estimate of density anomalies in the lower mantle4, and keep yield stress and chemical viscosity contrast constant (100 MPa and 10, respectively). We find the BMSs are fully entrained by ambient mantle materials, and subduction forms a great-circle girdle in small buoyancy ratio cases (B = 0.18 and 0.20). In large buoyancy ratio cases (B = 0.22, 0.26, and 0.30), subduction also forms a great-circle girdle, but BMSs form in 2 piles with different topographies and shapes. Thus, the adjustment of the buoyancy ratio in large buoyancy ratio cases has effects on the topography of BMSs but limited effects on the position of subduction zones, hence the plate tectonic configuration, and the stability of BMSs (Supplementary Figs. 3, 4).

Tomography study indicates that LLSVPs contain more bridgmanite than the ambient mantle4. MgSiO3 bridgmanite is more viscous than MgO periclase by up to 1000 times24,25. A chemical viscosity contrast of 10 for BMSs in our preferred model can decrease the viscosity difference between BMSs and the ambient mantle because the BMSs are hot and thermally less viscous26. We vary the chemical viscosity contrasts between the BMSs and the ambient mantle from 1–100 to test the influence of chemical viscosity on the pattern of BMSs (Supplementary Fig. 5). With increasing chemical viscosity contrast, the topography of BMSs rises, and the area of BMSs decreases, due to the decreasing efficiency of mantle convection and hence decreasing heat loss efficiency26. When the chemical viscosity contrast is >30, BMSs form three piles, and the position of subduction changes considerably. BMSs form two piles when the chemical viscosity contrast is <30. Note that the horizontal velocity of BMSs in these cases remains notably slower than that of the bulk mantle, indicating these BMSs are relatively sluggish (Supplementary Fig. 6).

---

## Methods

Thermochemical mantle convection models
We assume an anelastic and compressible fluid with an infinite Prandtl number, and we solve the non-dimensional equations of mass, momentum, heat, and chemical conservation in a 3D spherical shell on the Yin-Yang grid40 using the finite difference/volume code StagYY17. The main model setup used here is similar to that published previously18, and we further take plastic yielding into account to generate plate boundaries19,20. The reference Rayleigh number Ras is expressed as:

Ras = \rho s g\alpha \eta s \Delta T s D3 / \kappa 0 s, (1)

where \rho s is the surface density, g the gravity, \alpha the thermal expansion, \eta s the surface viscosity and \kappa 0 s the surface thermal diffusivity. In this study, Ras is fixed to 1 \times 108.

Temperature-, depth-, and composition-dependent viscosity coupled with plastic yielding is used. Meanwhile, we imposed a viscosity jump of 30 at 660 km depth. The viscosity is described fully by

\eta eff = 1 / (1/\eta(T,d,C) + 1/\eta Y), (2)

with

\eta(T,d,C) = \eta 0 (1+29H(d-660)) exp(VaD) exp(EaT+T off / (T+T s)) + KaC, (3)

and

\eta Y = (\sigma 0 + \sigma_ z) / 2\epsilon_ \Pi, (4)

where \eta Y is the yield viscosity, \sigma 0 the surface yield stress, \sigma_ z the yield stress gradient, which is set to 0 to introduce transform faults as suggested by previous study41, and \epsilon_ \Pi the second invariant of the strain rate tensor. H is the Heaviside step function, Va the non-dimensional activation volume, Ea the non-dimensional activation energy, T off the offset temperature, which is fixed to 0.88\Delta T s to reduce the temperature-induced viscosity variation at the surface, C the composition field, and Ka the parameter controlling the chemical viscosity contrast \Delta \eta C = exp(Ka). No prescribed plate boundaries are imposed and the yield stress help to generate plate-like behavior at the top of the domain. To avoid numerical problems, the viscosity is truncated between 10-3 and 105 of the reference viscosity.

Initial condition and model setup
To introduce basal mantle structures (BMSs), we initially setup an even dense layer above CMB whose thickness is 0.06 (173 km in dimensional unit)42,43. The grid resolution is 64 \times 192 \times 64 \times 2 with grid refinement at both the surface, the bottom, and at 660 km depth (the ringwoodite phase change to bridgmanite). The boundary conditions of the bottom and the top are free-slip, and the temperature of the top is set to 0.12 (300 K), and the bottom is 1.5 (3750 K) (Supplementary Fig. 8a). The model includes both internal and basal heating. The internal heating rate is 7.08 \times 10-12 W/kg, as suggested in ref. 44. Given the LLSVPs possibly enriched in heat-producing elements, we assume the heating rate of the BMS is ~7 times that of the ambient mantle materials26,45. The superadiabatic thermal boundary layers are located at the surface and the bottom, the thickness of which is ~87 km. Random temperature perturbation is implemented at both boundaries. The curvature of the shell f defined as the ratio between the radius of the core and the total radius is set to 0.55 corresponding to the Earth’s value. We use a tracer ratio method to track the compositional field46. Two types of tracers are used to represent the compositional field, where 0 corresponds to the ambient mantle, and 1 corresponds to BMS material. The number of total tracers of all models is 24 million, corresponding to about 15 tracers per cell, which is sufficient for simulating material entrainment46. The composition field is calculated from the ratio between BMS tracers and total tracers. The initial thickness of the BMS material is 0.06 (corresponding to 173 km), and the initial volume of the BMS material is ~3% of the mantle42,43. The density contrast between BMSs and the ambient mantle is controlled by the buoyancy ratio

B = \alpha s \rho s \Delta T s / \Delta \rho c, (5)

where \Delta \rho c is the density contrast between BMSs and the ambient mantle.

Detection of plumes and slabs
To determine plumes and subduction zones in our models, we calculate threshold temperatures of plumes and slabs following those of ref. 47, which assumes that a point is located within a plume (subduction zone) if the temperature at this point is higher (lower) than:

T p(d) = T avg(d) + fp(T max(d) - T avg(d)), (6)

T s(d) = T avg(d) + fs(T min(d) - T avg(d)), (7)

where T avg(d), T max(d) and T min(d) are the horizontally averaged, maximum, and minimum temperature at depth d, and fp and fs are fixed to 0.5 and 0.1, respectively, in this study.

Horizontal velocities of BMSs and plumes
The horizontal velocities of BMSs and plumes are defined as the root-mean-square averaged velocity within the BMSs and plumes at each depth by

V HBMSs(d) = \sqrt{ (\int C>0.5 V H2 dA) / (\int C>0.5 dA) }, (8)

V HPlumes(d) = \sqrt{ (\int T>Tp(d) V H2 dA) / (\int T>Tp(d) dA) }, (9)

where V H = (V\theta, V\phi) is the horizontal velocity at the point of (d, \theta, \phi), \theta colatitude, \phi longitude, dA infinitesimal area. The temporal variation of the horizontal velocity of BMS is calculated at each timestep by

V HBMSs = \sqrt{ (\int C>0.5 V H2 dV) / (\int C>0.5 dV) }, (10)

where dV is infinitesimal volume.

Vote maps of BMSs and plumes
To quantify the stability of BMSs, we calculate vote maps of BMSs following a similar strategy of ref. 48. For a given depth of the composition field, a binary threshold of 0 (no BMSs) or 1 (BMSs) is applied to every latitude-longitude pixel in each time slice within the period of time we selected, followed by a pixel-wise summation of all N time slices within the period selected. The pixels of the vote map hence take values between 0 and N. We then divided the value of each pixel on the vote map by N to get a normalized vote map on which all pixels take values between 0 and 1. A value of 0 on a vote map indicates no BMSs have existed in this pixel during the whole selected period of time, while a value of 1 indicates that BMSs have existed in this pixel at some point during the whole selected period of time, and a value between 0 and 1 indicates the normalized time length that BMSs have existed in this pixel compared to the selected period of time. Vote maps of plumes are calculated by using the same method in the temperature field.
